summary: A 1974 discussion and proposal for a common command language that users could use across different network services, called the Unified User-Level Protocol. The idea was to spare users from learning a different set of commands for every host. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 666 proposes a common set of commands that users could use across different network hosts. Servers could connect those commands to existing local functions, while the same command forms could also support programs.

questions: what was the unified user level protocol
subtitle: A common command language proposal for users and programs on network hosts.

tldr.problem: Users and programs had to deal with different command languages and service interfaces on different network hosts.
tldr.mechanism: The Unified User-Level Protocol proposes a common command subset for login, help, mail, file operations and program invocation, implemented by translating commands to each host's existing functions.
tldr.outcome: The document specifies a proposed command language and Telnet option context; it also notes unresolved details and makes some commands optional or speculative.

today: RFC 666 is a proposed 1974 specification for a common user-level command language across network servers.

sections.title: Why a Common Command Language
sections.content:
The proposal grows out of RFC 451's Unified User-Level Protocol idea and develops it as a common command language. The author says one shared command subset could let users invoke common functions, including batch jobs, across different server hosts without learning each host's command language.

The RFC also aims to support program-driven resource sharing and avoid requiring every host to implement a new responding protocol for each service. It proposes adding the commands to existing systems by translating them to native commands rather than replacing those systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal gives different hosts a shared set of commands for common tasks. Each host could connect those commands to its existing software instead of replacing it.

sections.title: Telnet Context and Common Commands
sections.content:
Initially, the UULP would be a Telnet option that a server could negotiate. The server would provide a common command environment, with a local command to leave it for the host's native command processor. The proposal defines commands for login, prompts and help; mail and user lookup; console-to-console communication; file operations; entering FTP or RJE; and invoking programs with call.

Commands and control arguments were designed for both users and programs. The RFC prefers constrained text responses rather than numeric response codes and allows command names in all upper- or all lowercase. It proposes a *free identifier for a supported sampling account if available.
sections.plainLanguage: A user would negotiate the Telnet option and then use shared commands for common work such as login, mail and files. The local command would return to the host's own command environment.

sections.title: Keeping the Interface Practical
sections.content:
The author emphasizes front-ending existing commands so hosts would not need to discard their current systems. The common language was intended to be directly usable by people as well as programs. Optional commands address differences in prompts, end-of-line, erase and kill characters, and case handling.

The RFC also discusses a generic login, help, mail, file manipulation, a proposed common editor called neted, and invocation of local or foreign programs. Some details, including batch processing and the editor commands, are explicitly left for further work.
sections.plainLanguage: The common commands were meant to fit around existing host software and terminal differences. The RFC leaves some areas, including parts of batch use and editing, open for more work.

sections.title: Limits and Status of the Specification
sections.content:
The document is a proposed specification and does not claim that every server implements the commands. Servers may respond that optional commands are not implemented. Several features are optional, and some mechanisms, such as up-to-date network-wide user names and secure database updates, are not specified here.

The UULP is described as a way to access common functions and invoke other programs, not as a complete replacement for each host's native command system or for specialized protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: This proposal does not require every server to support every command. It defines a common interface but leaves some mechanisms and implementation details unresolved.
